title: Andariel
summary: Andariel, also tracked as Onyx Sleet and Silent Chollima, is a North Korean state-linked cluster that public reporting attributes to a military intelligence bureau and describes as related to, but distinct from, the broader Lazarus activity set and the financially focused Bluenoroff cluster. Its documented history has a dual character: destructive attacks against South Korean banks, broadcasters and critical infrastructure, and financially motivated intrusion into cryptocurrency exchanges and payment systems. Reporting describes scanning and exploitation of internet-facing servers, including web application platforms, as well as spearphishing and supply chain abuse for access. Later reporting describes a shift toward ransomware-style extortion against healthcare and other organisations. Defenders see webshells on servers, credential theft, and lateral movement.

beginner.definition: Andariel is a name for attacks that public reports link to North Korea. The group has attacked banks and broadcasters and also stolen from cryptocurrency services. Some reports describe it using ransomware too, which is unusual for a state-linked group. It is often grouped with the wider Lazarus activity.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group shows that motives can mix. An attacker may spy, damage systems and steal money in the same year, or even the same campaign. If your plan only covers one of those cases, the others are gaps. The group also targets public-facing servers, which many teams watch less than user computers. Treating every motivation as possible keeps your defence honest.
howItWorks: The attackers scan for internet-facing servers that are out of date or badly configured.
They use a known weakness to run their own code on the server and keep access there.
They steal account details and reuse them to log in to other systems inside the network.
They use tools already installed on the system, so fewer new files appear on disk.
Depending on the goal, they copy data, disrupt services or move funds out.
In extortion cases they also encrypt files and demand payment to make recovery hard.
beginner.example: Imagine a warehouse with a small office at the front and a loading bay at the back. The thieves ignore the office and climb through the bay, then use the staff keys they find. They might steal goods, smash the shelves or demand payment to return the stock. One weak opening can serve several different plans.
takeaways: One group can have several motives, so plan for spying, disruption and theft together.
Internet-facing servers need patching and monitoring because they are a common first step.
Stolen credentials let an intruder look like a normal user, which is hard to spot.

objectives: Describe Andariel and the different motivations public reporting attributes to it.
Explain why a state-linked group might adopt criminal extortion methods.
Describe how exploitation of an internet-facing server leads to internal movement.
Identify the server-side evidence that would expose a webshell or implant.
Explain why threat classification by motive alone can leave defensive gaps.
Repeat public attribution for this cluster with source and confidence level.
